title: Parsing A Boolean Expression
description:
# Parsing A Boolean Expression

A boolean expression evaluates to either `true` or `false`. The input string is guaranteed to be a valid expression using only these forms:

* `t` evaluates to `true`.
* `f` evaluates to `false`.
* `!(subExpr)` evaluates to the logical NOT of one sub-expression.
* `&(subExpr1, subExpr2, ..., subExprn)` evaluates to the logical AND of one or more sub-expressions.
* `|(subExpr1, subExpr2, ..., subExprn)` evaluates to the logical OR of one or more sub-expressions.

Commas only separate operands inside `&` and `|`. Parentheses always belong to the immediately preceding operator.

Given `expression`, return the boolean value of the whole expression.

AND is true only when all operands are true; OR is true when at least one operand is true; NOT reverses true and false. For example, `!(t)` is false and `|(f,t)` is true.

## Example 1:

**Input:** expression = "&(|(f))"
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** `|(f)` is false, so `&(false)` is also false.

## Example 2:

**Input:** expression = "|(f,f,f,t)"
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** At least one operand of the OR expression is true.

## Example 3:

**Input:** expression = "!(&(f,t))"
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** `&(f,t)` is false, and negating it gives true.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= expression.length <= 20000`
* `expression[i]` is one of `(`, `)`, `&`, `|`, `!`, `t`, `f`, and `,`
* `expression` is syntactically valid
* `!` has exactly one operand
* `&` and `|` have at least one operand

solutions.name: Character Stack Reduction
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan the expression left to right. Ignore commas, push operators, opening parentheses, and boolean literals. When a closing parenthesis appears, pop all boolean literals for that call, pop the opening parenthesis and operator, reduce the call to one boolean literal, and push it back.

## Key Insight

Every closing parenthesis marks a complete sub-expression whose operands are already reduced to `t` or `f`. The stack therefore always stores unresolved outer context plus already-evaluated child values.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the expression length.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the stack.

solutions.name: Recursive Descent Parser
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep one index into the string and parse according to the grammar. Literals return immediately. For an operator, consume its opening parenthesis, recursively parse each child, combine child values, then consume the closing parenthesis.

## Key Insight

The expression grammar is prefix-form and fully parenthesized, so one moving index is enough. After each recursive call returns, the index is positioned at the next comma or closing parenthesis of the current operator.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n), because every character is consumed once.
- Space Complexity: O(d), where d is the nesting depth of the expression.

solutions.name: Operator Frame Stack
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent each open operator call as a frame. A frame stores its operator and whether any child value has been true or false. Literal values and completed child frames are fed into the parent frame, and a closing parenthesis reduces the top frame.

## Key Insight

AND, OR, and NOT do not need the exact list of children after the children are evaluated. A pair of flags, `hasTrue` and `hasFalse`, contains enough information to reduce the operator.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n).
- Space Complexity: O(d) frames for nesting depth d.

solutions.name: Short-Circuit Recursive Parser
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use recursive parsing, but once an `&` has seen a false child or a `|` has seen a true child, skip the remaining child expressions syntactically instead of evaluating them. Skipping still advances over nested parentheses correctly.

## Key Insight

Short-circuiting is safe only if the parser still consumes the entire expression. The result is decided early, but `skipExpression` preserves the invariant that the index lands on the next delimiter of the current operator.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n), since evaluated and skipped characters are each scanned once.
- Space Complexity: O(d), where d is nesting depth.

solutions.name: Primitive Array Frame Machine
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use primitive arrays instead of object frames. One array stores the operator for each nesting level, and another stores a two-bit mask: bit 0 means a false child has appeared, and bit 1 means a true child has appeared.

## Key Insight

The frame-stack idea can be made allocation-light. The same `hasTrue`/`hasFalse` information fits in two bits, so the parser can evaluate long expressions with predictable memory use.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n).
- Space Complexity: O(n) worst-case for the primitive stacks.
